newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OPEC's $30 billion windfall to smooth talks this week.
newsitem.headline: OPEC's $30 billion windfall to smooth talks this week.

text.p: OPEC oil ministers gathered in Vienna for a conference in buoyant mood thanks to an oil price rally which has boosted petroleum export revenues by nearly a quarter this year.

Responsible for maximising revenue flows to support their nations' oil-dependent economies, Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) ministers, who meet on Wednesday, are enjoying a windfall of unexpected proportions.

The cartel is set to earn a collective extra $30 billion of crude and petroleum product export revenues this year, with the help of a sustained oil price surge which has taken crude to six-year highs.

OPEC's 11 members should rake in oil export revenues of about $163 billion compared to $132 billion last year and $120 billion in 1994, according to Leo Drollas, chief economist at London's Centre for Global Energy Studies.

Increased revenues will allow debt-ridden OPEC producers, most of which made modest assumptions for oil prices in their budget projections, to eat into deficits, pay debts, ease financial reform programmes and spend on infrastructure.
Oil prices, at nearly $20 a barrel for benchmark Brent blend on average for the year so far, are running $3 ahead of last year.
OPEC crude production also is running higher as all members bar Saudi Arabia and it's Gulf allies the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait ignore output quotas and pump full steam.

Combined OPEC output this year looks likely to average about 25.8 million barrels a day (bpd) compared to 25.1 million in 1995 and 24.7 million in 1994, according to International Energy Agency (IEA) figures.
OPEC's leading producer, Saudi Arabia, having budgeted for $14 a barrel crude in January, has seen export values near $18.50.

Riyadh can count on a $10 billion excess to deal with a projected $4.9 billion deficit on spending of $40 billion this year, Henry Azzam, chief economist at the Jeddah-based National Commercial Bank said recently.
Saudi foreign currency reserves, run down during the 1990-1991 Gulf War, are being rebuilt and debts to contractors repaid.
In Iran hard currency receipts from oil sales are expected to exceed budget forecasts by more than $2 billion, oil minister Gholamreza Aghazadeh said in October.
Oil income was expected to exceed $18 billion compared to forecasts of $16 billion, Aghazadeh said.
Analysts say the final figure is likely to be nearer $19 billion.
Debt-ridden Venezuela is expected to reap about $3 billion more than projected, helped by higher oil output as well as increased prices, government officials say.
Caracas, which budgeted for $13.50 crude, has averaged more than $17 and has vowed to use the cash exclusively for the repayment of foreign debt to prevent inflation taking flight again.
Nigeria, making $4 a barrel more than the $16 for which it budgeted, can expect to raise about $12 billion, of which the government take is some 85 percent, up from $9.5 billion last year.
Abuja said it was spending on rebuilding its railways and financing a reserve account rather than servicing its $33 billion international debt.
Indonesia, setting a $16.50 budget for its relatively expensive light oil, is making an extra $600 million for every extra dollar a barrel, state oil company Pertamina says.
Set to earn about an excess $2 billion for the year, almost half will go on crude for its own refineries.
Troubled Algeria has been helped by oil export revenues approaching $5 billion for the year, up from $4 last year, the Centre for Global Energy Studies calculates.
Kuwait, having used a conservative $13 oil price in forecasting a 3.7 percent rise in oil revenues in fiscal 1996/1997 to $12.9 billion can expect to earn an extra $3 billion.
